sentences.text: Oviraptor was a small, feathered dinosaur estimated to be 1.6 to 2 meters long and weigh between 33 and 40 kilograms.
It possessed a wide lower jaw, a skull that likely featured a crest, and toothless jaws equipped with a horny beak.
The animal had well-developed, elongated arms ending in three fingers with curved claws.
Its hindlimbs were long, featuring four-toed feet where the first toe was reduced.
The first remains were collected in 1923 from the Djadokhta Formation in Mongolia during an expedition led by Roy Chapman Andrews at the Bayn Dzak locality.
Henry Fairfield Osborn formally described the genus and the species Oviraptor philoceratops in 1924, establishing it based on the holotype specimen AMNH 6517.
Oviraptorids likely brooded and protected their nests by crouching over them.

In 1977, Rinchen Barsbold proposed that Oviraptor used its robust jaws and beak to crush mollusk shells like clams, though David K. Smith rejected this in 1990, arguing the jaws preserved shearing surfaces rather than crushing mechanisms.
In 1995, Mary H. Norell and colleagues found lizard remains in the holotype's body cavity, suggesting Oviraptor was partially carnivorous.
In 1997, Rinchen Barsbold re-examined Oviraptor mongoliensis and determined it belonged to the new genus Rinchenia, though it remained an informal nomen dubium.
Traits of the Oviraptor skull suggest it belongs near the base of the Oviraptoridae family tree, distinct from more derived members.
Oviraptor lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically between 71 and 75 million years ago.

The Djadokhta landscape featured intermittent streams, seasonal moisture, and was occasionally affected by dust and sandstorms, with a climate thought to have shifted to a more humid fluvial environment later.
When described in 1924, Oviraptor was presumed to be ovivorous based on its discovery at a Protoceratops nest.
Rinchen Barsbold suggested Oviraptor had a semiaquatic lifestyle based on its diet and anatomy, a hypothesis later contested by others.
Stig Olav K. Jansen considered Oviraptor's lower jaws strong enough to crush eggs, nuts, or hard seeds, suggesting an omnivorous diet.
Persons and colleagues (2014) suggested that oviraptorosaurs were secondarily flightless and that tail traits may have been used for courtship displays.
